newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO agrees to 18-month mission in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO agrees to 18-month mission in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO agreed on Wednesday that its new Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia should stay in the country for no more than 18 months, with reviews every six months to decide needed troop levels.

Sources said NATO ambassadors had agreed in principle to a timetable outlined two weeks ago by U.S. President Bill Clinton for a follow-on force to replace the alliance's Implementation Force (IFOR) when its mandate expires on December 20.
"There's basic agreement...that we will be planning for 18 months," one source at North Atlantic Treaty Organisation headquarters said.
"That doesn't necessarily mean we will be staying for 18 months," the source added. "There will be reviews. Our aim is not to have any more troops there at any one time than is absolutely necessary."
NATO last week agreed to plan for about 30,000 international troops to stay on in Bosnia next year. But the issue of how long the new SFOR mission would stay was left undecided.
The alliance had been thinking in terms of one year, with France saying that two years may be needed.
But Clinton surprised America's allies on November 16 by saying the U.S. would keep its troops in Bosnia for 18 months, reviewing their presence every six months.

"There was a certain amount of consternation because everyone had been assuming a force for one year and the Americans...without any prior consultation, announced 18 months," Emyr Jones Parry, deputy political director at Britain's Foreign Office, said on Tuesday.
"There then followed an accelerated consideration in Brussels of what the Americans had proposed and how it should be taken forward," he told a parliamentary committee in London.
NATO sources insisted that the alliance would not be willing to remain forever in the region. "At the end of 18 months the mission will be finished," a NATO source said.
IFOR, which at its height had about 60,000 troops, was given a one-year mandate, which is effectively now being extended by the new, leaner force.
Alliance officials have in the past emphasised the need for deadlines, citing the 32 years of United Nations presence in Cyprus as an example of what it wants to avoid.
NATO sources said the ambassadors had also agreed a mandate for the new SFOR. It will be available for help with next year's muncipal elections and for some work on Bosnian reconstruction.
"Clearly (with fewer troops) it will have to be more selective," the source said.
But there was no question of the NATO-led force acting a Bosnia's policeman.
"We cannot and will not do police work. No police work," the source said, adding that this extended, as it does now, to not hunting down alleged war criminals.
